title: Seeing into the heart of Mira A and its partner
caption: The binary star Mira and its heart-shaped bubble, imaged by ALMA
credit: ESO/S. Ramstedt (Uppsala University, Sweden) & W. Vlemmings (Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A heart-shaped bubble sits at the centre of this ALMA image, part of a complex nebula around the binary star system Mira. Mira A ranks among the sky's best-known red giants, an old star already throwing the products of its life back into space to be recycled.

Its companion, Mira B, orbits it at twice the distance between the Sun and Neptune. Mira A has a slow wind that gently shapes the material around it. ALMA confirmed that Mira B is a very different star: a hot, dense white dwarf with a fierce, fast wind. The heart-shaped bubble is blown by Mira B's energetic wind inside Mira A's calmer outflow, and it formed within roughly the last 400 years.

Studying red giants tells astronomers about the Sun's future and how earlier stars spread the elements needed for life. Mira shows how double stars can shape their surroundings differently from single stars like the Sun.
scale: Mira lies about 400 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.

understand.summary: This image comes from ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, observing at submillimetre wavelengths around 900 microns. The source does not publish a colour mapping.
understand.eye: ALMA detects submillimetre radio waves, which the eye cannot see, so this is not a visible-light view.

explore: Other old, dying stars also have strange surroundings, but it is not always clear whether they are single or double. Mira's two stars have strongly affected each other despite their separation, leaving clues for scientists to decode.
alt: A complex nebula with a heart-shaped bubble at its centre around a pair of stars.
